summary: Provides guidelines for evaluating new congestion control algorithms for interactive point-to-point real-time media carried over RTP, as in telephony and video conferencing. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary:
This RFC explains how to test a new method for keeping real-time calls from jamming a network. It lists what to measure, which network conditions to test under, and what other traffic to run at the same time.

Its purpose is to make results comparable. Two different tests using the same settings can be compared, and two that do not cannot.

questions: how to evaluate rtp congestion control
what makes a good real-time congestion control test
what network parameters should be used to test real-time congestion control
how do you evaluate rtp congestion control
subtitle: The metrics, network settings and traffic models used to test new congestion control for interactive real-time media.

tldr.problem: A new way of avoiding network jams for voice and video calls has to be tested before anyone relies on it. Without a common method, two results cannot be compared.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC fixes the metrics to measure, the log format to record them in, the ranges of delay, loss and queue length to test over, the jitter models to apply, and the background traffic to run alongside.
tldr.outcome: It supplies the building blocks for the test cases in RFC 8867 and the wireless cases in RFC 8869. It defines no quality metrics, and passing the tests does not mean an algorithm is free of risk.

today: RFC 8868 is an Informational RFC and has not been obsoleted. It supplies the network parameters, traffic models and metrics that the test cases in RFC 8867 and the wireless cases in RFC 8869 build on. It defines no quality metrics, so results from it describe comparative performance only.

sections.title: What This Document Does and Does Not Cover
sections.content:
The RFC gives guidelines for evaluating new congestion control algorithms for interactive point-to-point real-time media. Congestion control is the part of a protocol that slows down sending when the network looks crowded. The requirements such algorithms must meet are set out in RFC 8836, and this document builds on RFC 5033 and RFC 5166.

The stated goals are to help prevent a congestion collapse, to promote fair use of capacity, and to optimise the throughput of the media flow. The algorithms evaluated are also expected to stay inside the envelope of the circuit breakers defined in RFC 8083.

The document covers only the network parameters and traffic models used in an evaluation. The minimal requirement for a congestion control proposal is to produce or present results for the test scenarios in RFC 8867; proponents may also produce results for the wireless scenarios in RFC 8869.

It does not cover the application side. No quality metrics are defined, because quality metrics and the ways of inferring them differ between media types and keep changing. The RFC does record a consensus that each algorithm should be able to show it is useful for interactive video, by analysis with real codecs, real video sequences and current quality metrics.
sections.plainLanguage:
Congestion control is the part of a protocol that slows down when the network looks full. This RFC says how to test a new version of it fairly.

It sets out what to measure and under which network conditions. It leaves out any measure of picture or sound quality, because that changes from one year to the next.

sections.title: The Metrics and the Packet Log
sections.content:
Each experiment is expected to log every packet that arrives and every packet that leaves, either inside the application or at the endpoints with a packet capture tool. The metrics are then computed from that log. The list runs from the basics, such as sending rate, receiver rate and goodput measured at 200 millisecond intervals, packets and bytes sent and received, packet delay, and packets lost or discarded by the playout buffer, through to post-repair loss when retransmission or forward error correction is used.

Fairness gets its own metric. Experiments must report the relative ratios of the average throughput obtained by each media stream, and, where cross-traffic such as TCP is present, the ratio between the media streams and the cross-traffic. The measurement interval should be set at a few values, for example 1, 5 and 20 seconds. As a general guideline, the relative ratio between congestion-controlled flows of the same priority and similar round-trip time should be bounded between 0.333 and 3.

Two further metrics describe behaviour over time: convergence time, which is the time taken to reach a stable rate after startup, after the link capacity changes, or when new flows are added, and instability, counted as the number of times the sending rate swings between a high and a low watermark in a defined window. The RFC gives an example of watermarks at 500 kilobits per second, 2 megabits per second and a window of 500 milliseconds.

All of this comes from one log format, given in Section 3.1. Each line holds a send or receive timestamp in seconds and microseconds, the RTP payload type, the synchronisation source identifier in hexadecimal, the RTP sequence number, the RTP timestamp, the marker bit and the payload size in bytes. Lines end with a carriage return and line feed, a carriage return or a line feed, and empty lines are ignored.
sections.plainLanguage:
Every test records each packet that goes in and out. From that record the RFC computes rates, delay, loss, fairness and stability.

It also fixes the format of the record, so that results from different testbeds can be compared afterwards.

sections.title: The Network Conditions to Test Over
sections.content:
The RFC lists the values implementors should choose first.

One-way propagation delay has four settings: very low at 0 to 1 milliseconds, low at 50 milliseconds, high at 150 milliseconds, and extreme at 300 milliseconds. Tests must show that the algorithm works across a broad range of path characteristics, including transcontinental and satellite links.

End-to-end loss has five settings: no loss at 0 percent, then 1, 5, 10 and 20 percent. Many paths today are largely lossless, but wireless interference, remote regions and fast mobility all produce substantial loss.

Drop-tail router queue length is measured as the time taken to drain the queue, and has three settings: quality-of-service aware or short at 70 milliseconds, nominal at 300 to 500 milliseconds, and buffer-bloated at 1000 to 2000 milliseconds. The RFC notes that core backbone queues are very short while home gateways tend to be longer. To convert a queue length in seconds to one in bytes, multiply the seconds by the throughput in bits per second and divide by eight.

Loss generation must at least use independent random losses, because that model needs the fewest parameters. More elaborate models are allowed, and the RFC names the Gilbert-Elliott model for correlated losses.

Jitter is handled with two bounded models. Random Bounded Packet Delay Variation (RBPDV) is presented for information only. Approximately Random Subject to No-Reordering Bounded PDV (NR-BPDV) must be used in the evaluation. It differs from the first model in one way: if a packet would end up earlier than the previous packet plus the serialisation delay at the bottleneck link, its time is pushed later, so packets never arrive out of order. The reason is that on real paths a late packet tends to hold up the packets behind it, which happens on mobile links with per-flow queues. The recommended distribution for the delay variation is a truncated Gaussian with a standard deviation of 5 milliseconds and a limit of 3 standard deviations.
sections.plainLanguage:
A test must cover slow and fast paths, clean and lossy paths, and short and long router queues. The RFC gives exact numbers for each.

It also defines how to add jitter, so that packets get delayed by a random amount. One of the two models keeps packets in order, and that one must be used.

sections.title: The Traffic to Run Alongside
sections.content:
TCP traffic is modelled in two ways. Long-lived flows download data throughout the session and are expected to have an endless supply, which roughly matches a software download. Short flows are a group of downloads separated by idle periods, and not all of them start together. The recommended model is that 30 connections start at once and fetch small amounts of data, 30 to 50 kilobytes each, spread evenly, which covers web page resources rather than video files. The gap between bursts is drawn from an exponential distribution with a mean of 10 seconds. Many congestion control schemes are in use, so experiments are encouraged to try a range, including CUBIC, and to document which schemes and parameters were used.

RTP video uses the two traffic models of RFC 8593, one that statistically characterises an encoder and one that plays back recorded traces. The recommended minimum is two video streams: Foreman at CIF resolution and FourPeople at 720p, both supplied as raw video to be encoded on the fly. Because the sequences are short, 300 and 600 frames respectively, they are stitched together repeatedly until the desired length is reached.

Background UDP is a constant bit rate flow. It sends at one rate for the whole session, or changes rate at set intervals, with the interval between packets worked out from the rate and the packet size. The packet size is normally the path maximum transmission unit, with a default of 1500 bytes. The RFC adds that newer transports such as QUIC use UDP but, because of their own congestion control, behave much like TCP, so they can be treated as the same kind of competing traffic.
sections.plainLanguage:
Real-time media is never alone on a link. The RFC describes three kinds of traffic to run next to it: web-style downloads, a video stream, and a steady UDP flow.

Using the same traffic every time is what makes two results comparable.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC is explicit that it is not itself subject to security considerations. It sets out evaluation criteria for comparing congestion control protocols, and the protocols evaluated may have their own security properties.

Two warnings follow. First, succeeding under all of the tests may be enough for a comparative evaluation, but must not be read as showing that the protocol is free of risk when deployed on the Internet. Evaluations are expected to run in controlled environments with a limited number of parallel flows, so by definition they cannot systematically consider every interaction or very large groups of communicating nodes under all circumstances. Careful protocol design is advised so that a proposal does not incidentally add traffic that could destabilise a network and cause a local congestion collapse.

Second, the specification looks at regular operation only. It does not suggest checks against malicious use by the sender, the receiver or intermediate parties, such as faked, dropped, replicated or modified congestion signals. It is left to each protocol specification to ensure that the authenticity, integrity and plausibility of received signals are checked, and that the right action, or no action, is taken.
sections.plainLanguage:
This RFC measures how well a congestion control method works under normal conditions. It does not test what happens when someone lies about the network state, and it says so plainly.

It also warns that passing the tests does not mean a method is safe on the open Internet, because the tests are small and controlled.
